body:
Why cyber safety matters

Mobile phones, computers and the Internet allow people to communicate, access government services, study, shop and transfer money without visiting an office. These activities depend on digital information, such as names, passwords, bank account details, messages and transaction records. Protecting this information is essential because its misuse can cause financial loss, loss of privacy or disruption of services.

Cybersecurity refers to protecting digital systems, networks, devices and information against cyber threats. Information security is the broader protection of information against unauthorised access, alteration or loss, whether the information is stored electronically or in another form. In everyday digital use, the 2 concepts overlap considerably.

Cyber safety for users means following practices that reduce the risk of online fraud, unauthorised account access, malicious software and loss of important digital information.

3 essential objectives of information security

Information security is commonly understood through confidentiality, integrity and availability. Each objective protects information in a different way.

  • Confidentiality: Information should be accessible only to authorised persons. If a criminal obtains a banking password or private medical record, confidentiality has been compromised.
  • Integrity: Information should remain accurate and should not be altered without authorisation. If a payment instruction is changed to send money to another account, integrity has been compromised.
  • Availability: Information and services should remain accessible to authorised users when needed. If ransomware locks important documents, availability has been compromised.

These objectives are related but not identical. For example, a file may remain available even after its contents have been secretly changed. Similarly, information can remain accurate while being disclosed to an unauthorised person.

How ordinary users become targets

A cyberattack does not always require a criminal to defeat technical protections. Sometimes the criminal persuades the user to perform an unsafe action. This manipulation is called social engineering.

Consider a message claiming that a bank account will be blocked unless the customer immediately shares a one-time password. The criminal is attempting to exploit fear and urgency. If the customer voluntarily reveals the code, the attacker may misuse it without needing to install malicious software on the customer's device.

Other attacks rely on software. A fraudulent application may secretly collect information, while ransomware may make files inaccessible. Consequently, cyber safety requires both safe user behaviour and protective measures such as strong authentication, software updates and backups.

Important distinction: Phishing is mainly a method of deception. Malware is malicious software. A phishing message may deliver malware, but the 2 terms do not mean the same thing.

Prelims focus

  • Cybersecurity protects digital devices, networks, systems and information.
  • Information security covers information in electronic and other forms.
  • Confidentiality concerns unauthorised disclosure.
  • Integrity concerns unauthorised alteration.
  • Availability concerns access to information or services when needed.
  • Trap: Every cyber fraud does not involve malware; some attacks depend on deceiving the user.

[NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 7, Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 52–53; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed p. 123; CERT-In, Frequently Asked Questions on Cyber Security Directions of 28 April 2022, May 2022, Section I, Questions 3–4 and Annexure-I, item (v), p. 17. Consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Cyber Safety: Protecting Information in Everyday Digital Life

body:
Meaning of malware

Malware is a shortened form of malicious software. It refers to software designed to carry out harmful or unauthorised activities, such as stealing information, interfering with normal operations, damaging files or preventing access to data.

Malware may reach a device through a deceptive application, an infected attachment, an unsafe download or an exploited software weakness. Some forms spread automatically, while others depend on a person installing or opening the malicious content.

Malware is software designed to infiltrate, damage, interfere with or misuse a digital system without the owner's informed consent.

Major types of malware

TypeDefining characteristicTypical consequence
VirusAttaches its code to another file or program and replicates when the infected content is executed.Spreads through infected files and may damage or alter data.
WormOperates as a standalone malicious program and can replicate to spread between systems.Spreads rapidly and may disrupt systems or networks.
Trojan horseMisleads the user about its true purpose by appearing legitimate or useful.May install harmful functions, steal information or allow unauthorised access.
SpywareSecretly observes or collects information about a user or device.May expose personal information, browsing activity or login details.
RansomwareBlocks access to files or systems, commonly by encrypting files, and demands payment.Makes information unavailable and may cause permanent data loss.

Virus versus worm

A virus is associated with another program or file. Its replication involves modifying or infecting other content. A worm is a standalone malicious program capable of replicating and spreading without attaching itself to another program. The difference concerns how the malicious software operates, not whether it is harmful.

Why a Trojan is different

A Trojan horse is defined principally by deception. For example, a criminal may distribute a fake banking application that appears to perform a genuine service but secretly gathers sensitive information. Unlike a virus or worm, a Trojan is not defined by its ability to replicate.

Spyware and ransomware

Spyware threatens confidentiality because it gathers information without the user's informed permission. Some malicious applications may also misuse device permissions or help a criminal observe sensitive activity.

Ransomware primarily threatens availability. The criminal blocks access to files, commonly by encryption, and demands money for restoring access. Paying the demand does not guarantee that the criminal will restore the files. Some ransomware attacks may also involve information theft, so confidentiality can be affected as well.

How users can reduce malware risks

  • Use genuine applications: Download software from trusted sources and check the publisher rather than following an unsolicited installation link.
  • Install security updates: Updates may correct weaknesses that attackers could exploit.
  • Be cautious with attachments: Unexpected files or links may contain malicious software even when they appear to come from a familiar organisation.
  • Use reputable security protection: Security tools can identify or block many threats, although no tool guarantees complete protection.
  • Maintain backups: A separate, usable copy of important files can reduce the consequences of ransomware or device failure.

Opening an unsafe link does not always mean malware has been installed. A link may instead lead to a fraudulent website that asks the user to enter a password or payment credential. The appropriate distinction is between malicious software and deceptive collection of information.

Prelims focus

  • Malware means malicious software.
  • A virus replicates by infecting other files or programs.
  • A worm is a standalone program capable of self-replication.
  • A Trojan misrepresents its true purpose.
  • Spyware gathers information; ransomware blocks access and demands payment.
  • Trap: Paying a ransomware demand does not guarantee recovery of files.

[CERT-In, Frequently Asked Questions on Cyber Security Directions of 28 April 2022, May 2022, Annexure-I, item (v), p. 17; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2022-0014, Mobile Based Malware: Methods and Countermeasures, 30 May 2022; CERT-In, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre, user safety guidance. Consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Malware: Viruses, Worms, Trojans, Spyware and Ransomware

body:
How phishing works

Phishing is a cyber fraud technique in which an attacker pretends to be a trustworthy person or organisation to obtain sensitive information or induce an unsafe action. The attacker may imitate a bank, payment service, delivery company, government department or familiar contact.

Phishing often works by creating a false reason for immediate action. A message may warn that an account will be frozen unless the user updates Know Your Customer information, commonly called KYC. It may direct the user to a fraudulent website that imitates the organisation's genuine website.

If the victim enters a password or one-time password on that page, the criminal may obtain the information needed to misuse the account. The apparent purpose is account verification; the real purpose is theft or deception.

Phishing methods classified by communication channel

MethodMain channelTypical example
PhishingOften email or fraudulent websites; also used as a broad term for deceptive communications.A fake bank message links to a false login page.
SmishingSMS or text message.A message claims an account will be blocked unless a link is opened.
VishingVoice call.A caller pretending to be a bank employee requests a password or OTP.

The common feature is deception. The terms smishing and vishing identify the communication method through which the deception is attempted.

Spoofing and impersonation

Spoofing means disguising the apparent origin or identity of a communication. For example, an attacker may make a message or caller identification appear to belong to a trusted organisation. A familiar-looking sender name or phone number is therefore not sufficient proof that the communication is genuine.

Warning signs of a phishing attempt

  • False urgency: Threats of immediate account closure, loss of benefits or a penalty unless action is taken at once.
  • Requests for secrets: Demands for passwords, OTPs, card PINs, UPI PINs or other confidential credentials.
  • Unverified links: Links that imitate an official website, contain unusual spellings or lead to an unfamiliar address.
  • Unexpected rewards: Claims that a prize, refund, cashback amount or benefit requires revealing a secret or making a payment first.
  • Unrequested software: Instructions to install an application or enable remote access for a supposed verification or refund.

HTTPS is not proof that a website is honest. An HTTPS connection helps protect information during transmission, but a fraudulent website can also use HTTPS. The identity and legitimacy of the website must still be checked.

Safe response to a suspicious message

The safest approach is to avoid using the contact details provided in the suspicious communication. Instead, open the bank's genuine application directly, type its known official website address or use a customer-service number obtained independently from an official source.

Do not share a password, OTP or UPI PIN with a caller, even if the person claims to be a bank officer or government employee. If an unexpected OTP arrives for an action the user did not initiate, it should not be communicated to anyone. For a banking transaction not initiated by the user, the bank should be informed through its official channel.

A person receives a text message stating that their bank account will be closed unless KYC details are updated immediately. The message contains a link and a phone number. The correct response is not to follow the message's instructions. The person should independently contact the bank through its genuine application, official website or branch to determine whether any action is required.

Prelims focus

  • Phishing uses deception to obtain information or induce unsafe action.
  • Smishing uses SMS or text messages.
  • Vishing uses voice calls.
  • Spoofing disguises the apparent identity or origin of a communication.
  • Fake KYC updates are a recognised method of financial fraud.
  • Trap: HTTPS or a familiar-looking sender name alone does not establish that a message or website is genuine.

[Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, Cyber Security Awareness Booklet for Citizens, Volume 1, 10 January 2020, discussion of phishing, vishing and smishing, p. 17; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, press release dated 28 January 2022, sections on phishing, vishing and safe digital banking practices; Reserve Bank of India, RBI Cautions Against Frauds in the Name of KYC Updation, 2 February 2024; CERT-In, Frequently Asked Questions on Cyber Security Directions, May 2022, Annexure-I, item (vii). Consulted 17 November 2026.]

body:
Why passwords are important

A password is a secret used to help establish that a person is authorised to access an account or service. A weak, predictable or reused password increases the risk that a criminal who learns it can enter the account.

Passwords protect many services, including email, online banking, digital learning platforms and social media. The security of an email account is particularly important because email is often used to receive account-recovery messages for other services.

Characteristics of a strong password

  • Length: Use a long password or passphrase. A passphrase consists of several words and can be easier to remember while remaining difficult to guess when the words are selected unpredictably.
  • Uniqueness: Use a different password for each important account. If one service suffers a data breach, a reused password may expose other accounts.
  • Unpredictability: Avoid names, birth dates, simple sequences, commonly used passwords and details that another person can easily discover.
  • Secrecy: Do not disclose passwords in response to phone calls, messages or emails. Avoid storing them in an openly accessible note.
  • Secure management: A reputable password manager can generate and store different long passwords. The password manager itself should be protected by strong authentication.

A password should be changed promptly if there is reason to believe it has been exposed or misused. Simply changing a weak password to another predictable password does not solve the underlying problem.

A password may contain uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols yet remain weak if it is short, predictable or reused. Length, unpredictability and uniqueness are essential considerations.

Authentication and authentication factors

Authentication is the process of checking whether someone is who they claim to be. A password is one authentication method, but additional methods can make unauthorised access more difficult.

FactorMeaningExample
KnowledgeSomething the user knows.Password or PIN.
PossessionSomething the user has.Registered phone, security key or authenticator device.
InherenceSomething the user is.Fingerprint or another biometric characteristic.

Two-factor authentication and multifactor authentication

Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires authentication using 2 different categories of factors. Multifactor authentication (MFA) is the broader term for authentication requiring multiple factors.

For example, a password combined with a code received through a registered phone can provide a knowledge factor and a possession factor. By contrast, asking for 2 different passwords does not ordinarily constitute 2-factor authentication because both passwords are knowledge factors.

An OTP, or one-time password, is a temporary code intended for a specific authentication or verification purpose. Unlike a regular account password, an OTP is valid for only one authentication or transaction. The user must not share an OTP with a stranger or enter it on an unverified website.

What 2FA can and cannot do

Suppose a criminal obtains a user's password through a fraudulent website. If the account also requires a separately controlled authentication factor, possession of the password alone may not be enough to gain access. This is why 2FA is valuable.

However, 2FA is not an absolute guarantee. A criminal may try to persuade the user to reveal an OTP or approve an authentication request that the user did not initiate. The additional factor must therefore remain under the legitimate user's control.

Password: a reusable secret for account access. OTP: a temporary code for a particular verification. 2FA: authentication that combines 2 different factor categories. These concepts are related but are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • A strong password should be long, unpredictable and unique to the account.
  • Reusing a password exposes multiple accounts if that password is compromised.
  • Knowledge, possession and inherence are the 3 major authentication factor categories.
  • 2FA uses 2 different factor categories.
  • OTP stands for one-time password.
  • Trap: Using 2 separate passwords is not, by itself, 2-factor authentication.

[CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2022-0026, Password Management and Security, issued 18 October 2022, sections on strong passwords, password management solutions and multifactor authentication; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, 28 January 2022, Safe Digital Banking Practices; CERT-In, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, password safety guidance. Consulted 17 November 2026.]
